short.en: Is each word a noun or a verb?

t.en: A new chapter, putting dynamic programming to work on sentences. In “he studies history”, “studies” is a verb; in “these studies”, it is a noun. How does a computer decide the part of speech of every word in a sentence?

Two clues: the cost of a word taking a given part of speech (“studies” is more often a verb, so that costs less), and the cost of one part of speech following another (a verb after a noun is natural, cost 0; another noun after a noun costs 3). The cost of the whole sentence is all of these added up. Pick the tagging with the smallest total cost.

It is a table again: rows are the three parts of speech, columns are the words of the sentence, and on the far left is “start”, holding 0. Cell (part of speech, word k) records: with the words before it tagged, and this word tagged as this part of speech, the least it can cost. The small number in a cell’s corner is the cost of this word taking this part of speech; × means it can’t.

Look only at the last step: the previous word could be any of the three parts of speech. For each possibility, which cell of the table and which fact in the This cell panel do you need? Of the three, which one do you want? The robot reads the previous word’s three cells with its telescopic arm; before the first word there is only “start”, so the arm reads just that cell, and the “after a noun” fact is then the cost of starting the sentence.

goal.en: Work out the smallest total cost of tagging the whole sentence: the cost of each word taking its part of speech, plus the cost of each pair of neighbouring parts of speech.

how.en: The This cell panel has the costs “after a noun / verb / adjective” and “this word, this tag”. Once you pass, see the tagging traced back from the table.

body.en: For every part of speech in every column, the table holds “the cheapest explanation up to here”. The smallest cell in the last column is the best tagging of the whole sentence; trace back along the green cells and you can read off each word’s part of speech.
This is the Viterbi algorithm. Speech recognition turning sound into words, and phone keyboards turning pinyin into Chinese words, both use this table: one column per moment, one row per possibility.

note.en: Viterbi: each row of the previous column + the cost of following it, take the min, then add the cost of tagging this word this way.

hints.en: If the previous word is a noun, the least cost up to it is in the “previous word as a noun” cell. Going on from there to this word, which cost do you add?
Take the min of the three, then add the “this word, this tag” cost.

note.en: “imports” was tagged as a verb: on its own, noun and verb cost the same; it was the words after it that made the verb win.
